library(dplyr)

s90 <- summ |> filter(alpha == 0.10) |> arrange(train_n)

  group_by(alpha) |> summarise(set_size = mean(set_size))

## Introduction

Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are a type of deep learning model designed to process grid-like data, such as images. An image is passed through layers of small filters that first detect simple patterns, such as edges and textures, and then combine them into progressively more complex ones. Because these filters are learned from data rather than hand-designed, CNNs have become the dominant approach to image recognition.

One field where CNNs have had a major impact is remote sensing, the analysis of images of Earth's surface captured from satellites and aircraft. Satellite missions such as Sentinel-2 image nearly all of Earth's land surface every few days in thirteen spectral bands, producing far more imagery than could be labeled by hand. Automatically classifying this imagery into land cover types, such as forest, farmland, water, or urban areas, supports applications from environmental monitoring to land-use planning, and CNNs have become the standard model for this task [@rao2026deep]. Applied to satellite imagery, their filters capture features such as field boundaries and shorelines, and they can draw on every spectral band rather than only the visible colors of an ordinary photograph.

One of the most widely used benchmarks for land cover classification is BigEarthNet, an archive of more than half a million Sentinel-2 image patches spanning ten European countries, released in 2019 [@8900532]. Each patch covers 1.2 × 1.2 km, is captured in 12 spectral bands, and can contain several of 19 land cover classes at once. This makes land cover classification on BigEarthNet a multi-label problem, in which a model must give an independent prediction for every class. This project uses the refined version of the dataset, BigEarthNet v2.0 [@clasen2025reben].

Despite their strong performance, CNNs report only a single prediction for each class, with a confidence score that is often unreliable: modern deep networks tend to be overconfident [@guo2017calibration]. This limitation matters most where training data is scarce, as it is for rare classes in BigEarthNet. The rarest class, "Beaches, dunes, sands," appears about 140 times less often than the most common, "Arable land," so the model is likely to be least reliable on exactly the classes it has seen least.

Conformal prediction addresses this by replacing a single prediction with a prediction set: a set of candidate labels guaranteed to contain the true label with a user-specified probability [@angelopoulos2023gentle]. The guarantee holds for any sample size, requires no assumptions about the data distribution beyond exchangeability, and applies to any model that outputs scores. The standard version uses one cutoff for all classes, so the guarantee holds only on average; the class-conditional version gives each class its own cutoff, so the guarantee holds for every class [@ding2023class]. This project applies class-conditional conformal prediction to a CNN trained on a stratified subset of BigEarthNet v2.0 and addresses three questions: (1) whether the resulting prediction sets achieve their target coverage for each land cover class, (2) how large the prediction sets are and how much each class contributes to them, and (3) whether variation in set size and coverage is systematically related to class frequency.

## Literature Review

### BigEarthNet and CNN Land Cover Classification

The original BigEarthNet labels were derived from the CORINE Land Cover map [@8900532]. BigEarthNet's refined successor, BigEarthNet v2.0, also called reBEN [@clasen2025reben], contains 549,488 patches. It rederived the labels from the 2018 CORINE map to correct label noise in the original release, and its geographic split addresses the spatial correlation between partitions in the original, which had made evaluation less reliable. These refinements reflect a broader recognition that satellite imagery behaves differently from the natural images on which most deep learning methods were developed, and that methods designed for it should account for its spectral, spatial, and geographic structure [@rolf2024mission].

The label distribution is highly imbalanced: in
BigEarthNet v2.0, "Arable land" appears in 188,025 patches, while
"Beaches, dunes, sands" appears in only 1,316, a roughly 140-fold
difference. Prior work on the dataset has achieved strong multi-label
performance with CNNs, including architectures that process spectral
bands in resolution-specific groups and show that different band groups
favor different land cover types [@9537619]. The same work identifies
severe class imbalance as its greatest limitation, which suggests that
headline accuracy figures may hide substantially weaker performance on
rare classes.

### Uncertainty in Deep Learning

@guo2017calibration found that modern deep networks are considerably less well calibrated than earlier, smaller networks, even as their accuracy has improved. In
remote sensing, this gap between apparent and actual reliability is
rarely addressed. A review of widely used Earth observation datasets
found that only about one in five included any uncertainty information,
and that the methods used were often unreliable [@singh2024uncertainty].
A recent survey of deep learning in remote sensing likewise identifies
uncertainty quantification as an underdeveloped area of the field
[@rao2026deep].

### Conformal Prediction

Conformal prediction provides a framework for attaching statistically valid uncertainty to the predictions of any model [@angelopoulos2023gentle]. In its common split form, the procedure is applied after training using a held-out calibration set, so it adds little computational cost. The framework has been extended to multi-label classification, where the goal is to cover the full set of labels present in each instance [@cauchois2021knowing].

Conformal prediction has begun to appear in remote sensing.
@valle2023quantifying applied it to pixel-level land use and land cover
classification and showed that prediction set size serves as a usable
indicator of classification uncertainty, and @singh2024uncertainty
demonstrated it on global land cover and tree species mapping. However,
the standard procedure guarantees coverage only on average across all
predictions. @ding2023class show that under class imbalance, this
average guarantee can conceal systematic over-coverage of common classes
and under-coverage of rare ones. Class-conditional conformal prediction
addresses this by calibrating a separate threshold for each class,
guaranteeing coverage within every class. The cost is that each
threshold is estimated only from that class's calibration examples, so
rare classes yield noisier thresholds and potentially larger, less
informative prediction sets. How this tradeoff plays out in multi-label
satellite image classification, where imbalance is extreme and
calibration data for rare classes is limited, has received little
attention.

## Methods

### Model

Classification used a convolutional neural network (CNN), which learns
spatial and spectral patterns directly from the image bands rather than
relying on hand-designed features. The network uses the four-block
filter progression of @9537619 on BigEarthNet: convolutional blocks with
32, 64, 128, and 256 filters, each followed by batch normalization,
ReLU activation, and max pooling, which progressively extract more
complex features. A global average pooling layer, a dropout layer (rate
0.3), and an output layer with one unit for each of the 19 classes
follow. A small architecture, with 397,811 parameters, was chosen
because training runs on a CPU, where a larger network would be slow and
more likely to overfit.

Because the task is multi-label, each output unit uses a sigmoid
activation, producing an independent probability for its class, rather
than a softmax activation, which forces probabilities to sum to one
across classes. The model was trained to minimize binary cross-entropy,
which penalizes the model for each class it predicts incorrectly, using
the Adam optimizer (learning rate 0.001, batch size 32) for up to 50
epochs. Training stopped early when validation loss failed to improve
for five consecutive epochs, and the weights from the best epoch were
kept. The model was implemented in R using keras3 with TensorFlow, and all code for sampling, preprocessing, model training, and conformal prediction is available in the [project repository](https://github.com/cghaveyUWF/IDC6940_GeospatialStat).

### Conformal Prediction

Conformal prediction converts the model’s probabilities into prediction
sets, lists of classes that are guaranteed to include each true class a
chosen percentage of the time [@angelopoulos2023gentle]. This study uses
the class-conditional version, which sets a separate threshold for each
class. The standard version guarantees coverage only on average across
all classes, which can hide poor coverage of rare classes
[@ding2023class], and that is the behavior this study examines.

The procedure is as follows:

1.  Randomly split the test patches into two equal halves: a calibration
    set and an evaluation set. Neither half is used in training.
2.  Run the trained model on the calibration set.
3.  For each class, take the calibration patches that truly contain that
    class and compute a score for each one: $$s = 1 - \hat{p}$$ where
    $\hat{p}$ is the probability the model gave to that class. A low
    score means the model was confident and correct.
4.  For each class, set a threshold $\hat{q}$ at the score below which
    90% of that class’s calibration scores fall, slightly adjusted
    upward to account for the finite sample size
    [@angelopoulos2023gentle].
5.  For each evaluation patch, include a class in its prediction set if
    the patch’s score for that class is at or below the class threshold:
    $$\text{include class } k \text{ if } \; 1 - \hat{p}_k \le \hat{q}_k$$
6.  Repeat steps 1–5 over 100 random splits and average the results
    across splits.
7.  Repeat the full procedure at 95% and 80% target coverage to see how
    the results change.

Because the calibration and evaluation patches come from the same random
split, this procedure guarantees that each class present in a patch is
included in its prediction set at least 90% of the time, on average
across patches.

### Evaluation

Classification performance was measured on the full test partition with F1 scores (the harmonic mean of precision and recall), a standard metric for multi-label image classification [@8900532], counting a class as predicted when its probability was at least 0.5. Macro-averaged F1 weights every class equally and therefore reflects performance on rare classes, while micro-averaged F1 is dominated by common classes.

The prediction sets were evaluated on the evaluation halves with the
following measures:

-   Coverage: for each class, the percentage of evaluation patches
    containing that class whose prediction set included it. Coverage at
    or above 90% means the guarantee held.
    $$\text{Coverage}_k = \frac{\text{patches containing class } k \text{ with } k \text{ in the prediction set}}{\text{patches containing class } k}$$
-   Coverage variability: the standard deviation of each class’s
    coverage across the 100 splits, measuring how stable the guarantee
    is from one calibration to the next.
-   Set size: the number of classes in each prediction set, averaged
    over evaluation patches. Smaller sets indicate a more confident
    model.
-   Minimum inclusion probability: for each class, the lowest
    probability at which the class enters a prediction set
    ($1 - \hat{q}_k$).
-   False inclusion rate: for each class, the share of evaluation
    patches without that class whose prediction set included it anyway.

To test whether uncertainty is linked to class frequency, each per-class
measure (minimum inclusion probability, false inclusion rate, coverage,
and coverage variability) was compared with the class’s number of
training patches using Spearman rank correlation, which does not assume a straight-line relationship, with significance assessed at the 0.05 level.

## Analysis and Results

### Data and Visualization

This study uses the Sentinel-2 portion of BigEarthNet v2.0 [@clasen2025reben], whose 12 spectral bands are recorded at 10, 20, and 60 m resolution. The metadata lists 480,038 patches after
excluding those covered by snow, clouds, or cloud shadow, each assigned
to an official train, validation, or test partition. These partitions
were used as provided, so the model is evaluated on patches from
different geographic areas than those it was trained on.

Because of computational constraints, a stratified subset was drawn from
each partition: up to 500 patches per class from the training partition,
400 from the test partition, and 100 from the validation partition.
Stratifying by class ensures that rare classes appear in every
partition, which simple random sampling would not guarantee. For the two
rarest classes, "Coastal wetlands" and "Beaches, dunes, sands," the test
partition contains fewer patches than the cap, so all available test
patches were included. Because each patch keeps all of its labels,
common classes that co-occur with rare ones exceed the per-class cap.
The final subset contains 18,065 patches (9,293 train, 1,885 validation, 6,887 test), with at least 516
training, 119 validation, and 117 test patches per class.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-counts
#| tbl-cap: "Patches per land cover class in the sampled subset."
knitr::kable(read.csv("outputs/class_counts.csv", check.names = FALSE))

```

Stratification substantially reduces, but does not remove, the class
imbalance. In the full dataset, the most common class appears about
143 times as often
as the rarest; in the training subset, the ratio is about
7.

```{r}
#| label: fig-imbalance
#| fig-cap: "Number of patches per class in the full dataset and in the training subset (log scale)."
#| fig-height: 7
full_counts |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(c(Full, Train), names_to = "Set", values_to = "n") |>
  mutate(Set = recode(Set, Full = "Full dataset", Train = "Training subset"),
         Class = reorder(Class, n, max)) |>
  ggplot(aes(n, Class, colour = Set)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::comma) +
  scale_y_discrete(labels = function(x) vapply(x, function(s)
    paste(strwrap(s, 40), collapse = "\n"), "")) +
  labs(x = "Patches containing the class", y = NULL, colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

```

Before training, the 20 m and 60 m bands were resampled to match the 10
m bands using bilinear interpolation, producing a 120 × 120 pixel image
with 12 bands for each patch. Each band was then standardized using the
mean and standard deviation of the training subset, which puts all bands
on a comparable scale and helps the model train. Standardization was
implemented as the network’s first layer, using only training
statistics, so that no information from the validation or test data
influenced the model.

### Statistical Modeling

#### Classification Performance

Training stopped early after 12 epochs, with the lowest
validation loss at epoch 7. On the full test partition, the
model reached a macro-averaged F1 of 0.507 and a
micro-averaged F1 of 0.573. The gap between the
two indicates weaker performance on less common classes.

#### Coverage

At the 90% target, average coverage across the 100 calibration splits
was between 0.897 and
0.909 for every class. Coverage held
for rare and common classes alike, and average coverage was not related
to training frequency (rho = 0.16, p = 0.514).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-results
#| tbl-cap: "Per-class conformal prediction results at 90% target coverage, averaged over 100 calibration splits. Classes are ordered from rarest to most common in training."
s90 |>
  transmute(Class = class, Train = train_n, Calibration = round(n_cal),
            `Min. probability` = round(min_prob, 3),
            Coverage = round(coverage, 3),
            `Coverage SD` = round(coverage_sd, 3),
            `False inclusion` = round(false_incl, 3)) |>
  knitr::kable()

```

Although average coverage was consistent, coverage varied more from
split to split for rare classes. The standard deviation of coverage
ranged from 0.010 to 0.052 and was strongly negatively
correlated with training frequency (rho = -0.94, p < 0.001). The two rarest
classes, with fewer than 80 calibration patches each, had the most
variable coverage.

```{r}
#| label: fig-coverage-sd
#| fig-cap: "Variability of class coverage across 100 calibration splits, by number of calibration patches (log scale), at 90% target coverage."
ggplot(s90, aes(n_cal, coverage_sd)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Calibration patches containing the class",
       y = "Coverage standard deviation") +
  theme_minimal()
```

#### Prediction Set Size

Prediction sets were large. At 90% target coverage, sets contained an
average of 9.3 of the 19 classes. Raising the target to 95%
increased the average to 11.4, and lowering it to 80% reduced it
to 6.7.

```{r}
#| label: fig-set-size
#| fig-cap: "Average prediction set size by target coverage level."
ggplot(set_sizes, aes(factor(paste0((1 - alpha) * 100, "%")), set_size)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6) +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(set_size, 1)), vjust = -0.4) +
  labs(x = "Target coverage", y = "Average set size (of 19 classes)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

The cost of inclusion differed widely between classes. False inclusion rates, the share of patches without a class whose set included it anyway, ranged from 5% ("Marine waters") to 77% ("Beaches, dunes, sands"). The false inclusion rate was not significantly related to training frequency (rho = 0.27, p = 0.260).

Set size therefore depended less on which classes a patch contained than on how many classes the model could not rule out, with classes such as "Beaches, dunes, sands" inflating sets far more than others.

#### Class Frequency and Inclusion Threshold

The minimum probability required for a class to enter a prediction set increased with training frequency (rho = 0.68, p = 0.001). Rare classes were included at very low probabilities, as low as 0.3% for "Beaches, dunes, sands", while common classes required up to 30%.

```{r}
#| label: fig-min-prob
#| fig-cap: "Minimum probability required for inclusion in a prediction set, by number of training patches (log scale), at 90% target coverage."
highlight <- c("Beaches, dunes, sands", "Coastal wetlands", "Marine waters", "Arable land")
ggplot(s90, aes(train_n, min_prob)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  geom_text(data = subset(s90, class %in% highlight),
            aes(label = class,
                hjust = ifelse(train_n < median(s90$train_n), 0, 1)),
            vjust = -0.8, size = 3) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Training patches containing the class",
       y = "Minimum inclusion probability") +
  theme_minimal()

```

## Conclusion

This project applied class-conditional conformal prediction to a
convolutional neural network trained on a stratified subset of
BigEarthNet v2.0, to examine whether prediction sets remain reliable
across land cover classes that differ widely in frequency. The guarantee held as designed: averaged over 100 calibration splits, every class achieved coverage within one percentage point of the 90% target, rare and common classes alike. The cost of that guarantee was high, however. With a modest classifier (macro F1 of 0.51), prediction sets contained an average of 9.3 of the 19 classes, which limits how informative an individual set is.

Class frequency shaped how the guarantee was achieved rather than whether it was achieved. Rare classes entered prediction sets at very low model probabilities, as low as 0.3% for “Beaches, dunes, sands,” reflecting the model’s low confidence even on patches where these classes were present. Rare classes also had far less stable coverage from one calibration split to the next (rho = -0.94, p < 0.001), because their thresholds were estimated from few calibration examples. In practice, this means that the coverage guarantee for a rare class is correct on average but less dependable in any single calibration, which is the situation a practitioner faces when calibrating once on the data available.

These results come with several limitations. The model was a small CNN
trained on a CPU with a subset of the data, and stratified sampling
reduced the class imbalance from roughly 140-fold in the full dataset to
roughly 7-fold in the training subset. Training on the full dataset with
a larger model would likely improve classification performance and
shrink prediction sets, but it would not add calibration data for the
rarest classes, whose test partitions were already used in full. Future
work could address this directly with methods that pool calibration data
across similar classes, such as clustered conformal prediction
[@ding2023class], which is designed for classes with limited calibration
data.
